Supervisor's note, accounts team, Friday
Tenzin has been restless all week. On Monday he mentioned an online 'task job': like videos, earn commission. He'd paid a 500-rupee deposit, got 700 back, and was cheerful about it.
On Wednesday he paid 5,000 to reach 'level two'. Today he asked me for a salary advance. When I asked why, he said the site had frozen his earnings until he deposits 20,000 more. 'If I stop now, the whole 5,500 is gone, ma'am. I just need to get it back.' His voice cracked on 'back'.
I did not approve the advance. I sat with him, told him this pattern is a known scam and has nothing to do with being careless. He agreed to call his bank with me after lunch and to tell his brother tonight.
- Nirmala

qa.a: It suggests he is desperate and ashamed, clinging to the hope of recovering the 5,500 rather than admitting it may already be lost.

qa.a: She refuses the advance, names the pattern without blaming him, and stays with him while he calls his bank and plans to tell his brother, so he stops feeding the loss.

qa.a: Nirmala may feel uneasy saying no to someone so upset, but she can see that the money would only fund the next demand.

Tuesday night
Paid the 8,500 today. Told myself it's the last one.
Recap, so I stop spinning: the 'customs office' said the parcel from my online friend was stuck, fee 999. Fine. Then a clearance certificate, 8,500, 'fully refundable on delivery'. If I didn't pay, the 999 was wasted and the parcel would be 'seized'.
So I paid 8,500 to protect 999. Written down, it looks ridiculous. In my head at 3 pm it looked like the only way out.
Samir asked why I've skipped dinner two nights running. Said work stress. I'm not ready for the look on Samir's face.
Now they want one 'final release charge'.
Kunal, you are not someone who gets scammed. That's what I keep repeating. It sounds less true every time.

qa.a: The first customs fee was 999.

qa.a: Kunal is afraid of the look on Samir's face and of admitting a mistake, so 'work stress' feels safer than the truth.

It started with liking videos for money. On day one Sahil earned ₹150 into his account, real money, for ten minutes of tapping. On day two the task group moved him to "prepaid tasks": pay ₹1,000, get back ₹1,300. It worked. Then ₹5,000. The dashboard showed ₹6,800.
Then the dashboard froze. "Error in your task. To unlock your balance, complete one VIP task."
Sahil stared at the screen in his Bengaluru PG. The dashboard said ₹31,000 was his, waiting. If he stopped now, he'd lose everything he'd put in. He borrowed on his credit card and sent it.
The next message asked for more, to "clear tax".
His roommate Akash asked why he wasn't eating. Sahil said, "Work stress." He couldn't say the truth out loud. Admitting it would mean the ₹31,000 had never been real, and that he had been a fool.

qa.a: Pay ₹1,000, get back ₹1,300.

qa.a: He felt ashamed and trapped, since admitting it meant the money on the dashboard had never been real.

qa.q: What turning point is still open to Sahil?
qa.a: Stop paying, screenshot everything, tell Akash, and report it to his bank and the cyber-crime helpline right away.

qa.q: What might Akash be sensing when Sahil stops eating?
qa.a: Akash senses something is wrong and feels concerned, though Sahil hides it as work stress.

grounding: After small early payouts a young man feels committed and pays more to recover his money, too ashamed to admit the mistake.

"Office work."
"Office work doesn't make you cry."
Lavanya put the phone face down. "It's the loan. The business loan I told you about."
"You said you'd dropped that idea."

"Fifty-five? And the loan?"
"It's approved! They just need one final release fee. After that it all comes back with the loan."
"Lavanya..."
"Don't. If I stop now, fifty-five thousand is simply gone. I can't tell Amma I lost that. I can't tell anyone." She wiped her eyes. "One more payment and it's over."
Lalit sat down slowly beside her. "Show me the messages."

I'm Mohit, and I want to explain the part people never understand: why I kept paying.
The first transfer was small, ₹2,000, for a trading course a friendly man recommended in a group chat. The next week my account showed profits. To withdraw them, there was a fee. Then a "wallet upgrade". Then a "clearance charge". Each payment was bigger than the last.
By then I'd put in more than ₹90,000. Every time I thought of stopping, I felt sick: stopping meant saying out loud that I, the one my family called sensible, had been fooled. Paying one more time felt less painful than admitting it.
That's what they count on. Not greed. Pride.
It only stopped when I asked my old friend Pankaj to lend me money for the "final fee", and Pankaj said, "I'll give you nothing for that. But I'll sit with you while you call the bank."

qa.q: What was the first transfer for?
qa.a: A trading course a friendly man recommended.

qa.q: Why did paying one more time feel less painful to Mohit?
qa.a: Mohit felt ashamed at the thought of admitting being fooled, so each new payment felt easier than facing the loss.

qa.q: What did Pankaj do that finally helped?
qa.a: Refused to fund the 'final fee' but offered to sit with Mohit while calling the bank, turning shame into action.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have felt when asked for money for the final fee?
qa.a: Pankaj probably felt alarmed and sad for a friend, and firm enough to say no while staying close.

grounding: A young adult recalls paying bigger and bigger fees to recover a first loss, because admitting the mistake felt worse than paying.

Note by Darshan, shift supervisor, packing unit, Thursday
Pranav came to me at lunch looking grey. On Monday he paid Rs 500 to "release" a parcel held at customs. On Tuesday they said the parcel needed insurance, so he paid 3,000. Today they asked for 12,000, a refundable clearance, and he had already started the transfer.
I asked why he kept going. He said, "If I stop now, the first two payments are wasted. And I'd have to tell my wife I was fooled." He kept saying he was not stupid.
What I did next: I told him plainly that the money already sent was probably lost, and that sending more would not bring it back. He cancelled the transfer in front of me. We called his bank on the number on the passbook, and I stayed while he filed a complaint on the cybercrime portal. I have given him the afternoon off to talk to his wife.

qa.q: How much did Pranav pay on Tuesday?
qa.a: On Tuesday he paid 3,000 for the parcel's insurance.

qa.q: What feelings kept pushing Pranav to pay more?
qa.a: He felt trapped and ashamed, afraid that stopping would waste the first two payments and that he would have to admit to his wife he was fooled.

qa.q: What turning point did the supervisor create, and why did it help?
qa.a: The supervisor said the money already sent was probably lost, which freed Pranav to cancel the transfer and report it the same day instead of chasing the loss.

qa.q: How might Pranav's wife be affected when he tells her?
qa.a: She may feel shocked and worried about the money, but hearing it that afternoon means they can face it together instead of him hiding more payments.

grounding: Shows a victim paying more after a small first transfer, trapped by the wish to recover losses and avoid admitting a mistake.
